title: August and the Choir
premise: Tamsin Marchetti, an exiled storm-caller hiding among smugglers in the Thornfell mountains, discovers that the border wards fell because the king of Vaelhar has been slowly consumed by a star-eating entity called the Choir, which silenced the night sky to sing the kingdom to sleep. Guided by a disgraced court astronomer and a ward-breaker who was once his closest friend, Tamsin must reach the capital before the Choir completes its song at the winter solstice. He learns the Choir was originally bound by the first storm-callers, whose order he was exiled from for refusing to sacrifice a child to renew the binding. In the end, Tasmim renews the binding not with a life but with his own exile made permanent—giving up his storms and his name—while the found family he gathered refuses to let him vanish, anchoring him with memory instead of magic.
about_author: Beatrix Villalobos is the pen name of a former mountain guide who writes fantasy shaped by years of leading travelers through treacherous passes. She lives in a stone farmhouse with too many cats and a stubborn belief that every villain thinks they're singing a lullaby.

chapters.title: The Night the Stars Went Out
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Smuggling salt through Thornfell's high passes, Tamsin notices the stars vanish one by one and feels his storm-magic go eerily quiet. The border wards collapse with a sound like breaking glass. Emotional beat: dread beneath practiced calm—the invisibility he built his life on is failing.

chapters.title: Salt and Ash
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He reaches the smuggler haven of Lowmark and finds refugees pouring through the fallen border, whispering that the king's soldiers sing in their sleep. His old friend Odessa Vane, now a ward-breaker, recognizes him despite his exile. Emotional beat: reluctant reconnection; the past he fled has found him.

chapters.title: What Odessa Broke
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. Odessa reveals she broke the wards under coercion—the Choir's agents hold her sister. She offers Tamsin a bargain: help her reach the capital, and she'll clear his name with the storm-caller order. Emotional beat: guilt and calculation; trust extended with trembling hands.

chapters.title: The Astronomer in the Cellar
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In Lowmark's flooded cellar-library, they find Master Ilen Corvane, a court astronomer who faked his death. He explains the Choir: a star-devouring chorus bound by the first storm-callers, now wearing King Aldric like a crown. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into horror as the scale of the threat becomes clear.

chapters.title: Roads That Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The trio takes a smuggler's road that shifts with the mountain's mood. Tamsin's dormant storms flicker when the Choir's hunters—grey-cloaked, humming—attack. Emotional beat: terror of his own power, and the first spark of the strength he'll need.

chapters.title: The Child Who Hums
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. They shelter a refugee caravan and find a mute girl, Brann, who hums the Choir's melody without being taken. Ilen believes she's a natural anchor. Odessa, remembering her sister, refuses to treat the girl as a tool. Emotional beat: tenderness against pragmatism; the theme of sacrifice introduced.

chapters.title: Exile's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Flashback woven through present: Tamsin's trial before the storm-caller order, his refusal to bind a child into the old binding, his exile. Present-day Tamsin realizes the Choir exploits the order's cruelty. Emotional beat: shame reframed as principle; his exile was a choice worth making.

chapters.title: The Grey Choir on the Pass
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Hunters corner them at a frozen pass. Tamsin unleashes a true storm for the first time in years—devastating, intoxicating, and noticed by every Choir agent in the mountains. Emotional beat: exhilaration shadowed by the knowledge that visibility means death.

chapters.title: What the King Remembers
chapters.summary: King Aldric's POV (brief, interlude). Inside the palace, Aldric surfaces from the Choir's song for ninety seconds, scrawling a warning: 'the binding wants a voice, not a life.' Then he drowns again. Emotional beat: claustrophobic pity; the king is a prisoner, not a villain.

chapters.title: The City That Sleeps Standing
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They reach the capital Vaelhar, where citizens work and smile with vacant harmony. Odessa infiltrates via her sister's captors; Ilen contacts old colleagues; Tamsin walks the streets unrecognized. Emotional beat: uncanny wrongness; home and horror intertwined.

chapters.title: Sister, Sister
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. Odessa finds her sister alive but half-dissolved into the Choir, content and hollow. She must choose: pull her out and break her, or leave her singing. She pulls. Emotional beat: grief without rescue; found family means choosing people who can't be saved whole.

chapters.title: The Order's Last Choirboy
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin seeks the storm-caller order's hidden chapter house and finds it massacred—except Elder Maren, the woman who sentenced him. She confesses the order knew the binding was failing for decades and hid it. Emotional beat: rage and bitter vindication; institutions rot before monsters arrive.

chapters.title: A Voice, Not a Life
chapters.summary: Ilen's POV. Ilen deciphers the first binding: it requires a voice willingly given, sustained by memory and love—the child sacrifice was a corruption added by frightened generations. Brann's humming is the key: she can hold the melody while a storm-caller sings the counter-song. Emotional beat: hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: The Solstice Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Three days to solstice. The group rehearses the counter-song in the catacombs; Tamsin's voice cracks on the high harmony and Brann corrects him, patient as a teacher. Emotional beat: quiet domestic warmth before the storm; found family crystallizes.

chapters.title: Odessa's Price
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. Odessa's sister, half-Choir, betrays their location to save what's left of herself. Grey hunters flood the catacombs. Odessa holds the tunnel alone so the others can escape, and is taken. Emotional beat: sacrifice as choice, not tragedy; she goes singing so they'll know where she is.

chapters.title: The Crowned Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Solstice eve. Tamsin infiltrates the throne room and faces the Choir wearing Aldric—its song peels memories from his mind as he approaches. He nearly forgets Odessa's name, then Lowmark, then his mother's face. Emotional beat: the price of survival made literal; memory as resistance.

chapters.title: Counter-Song
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Climax. Brann begins the anchor melody; Tamsin sings the counter-song while the Choir unmakes him memory by memory. He offers not a life but his name, his exile, his storms—everything that made him invisible. The Choir, starved for a willing voice, accepts. Emotional beat: transcendence through surrender; power renounced defeats power corrupted.

chapters.title: The King in the Empty Room
chapters.summary: King Aldric's POV. Aldric wakes in his own body, the Choir unbound, stars returning one by one through the windows. He finds Tamsin sitting blank-eyed on the steps, remembering nothing. Emotional beat: hollow victory; the savior who saved everyone but himself.

chapters.title: Names in the Ash
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. Odessa escapes her captors in the chaos and returns to find a man who doesn't know her. She tells him his story anyway—every night, patiently. Ilen and Brann join. Emotional beat: grief transformed into ritual; memory given back as gift, not restoration.

chapters.title: What the Storm Left
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Fragments return—not through magic but through love: the smell of salt, Odessa's laugh, Brann's humming. His storms do not return, and he finds he doesn't want them. Emotional beat: healing as slow weather; identity rebuilt from relationships rather than power.

chapters.title: The Choir's Last Note
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The unbound Choir, diminished, offers Tamsin a bargain: his storms and name back if he becomes its new crown-bearer. He refuses and sings it, instead, into quiet dissolution—Brann's melody softening it into starlight. Emotional beat: final temptation refused; the theme resolved—power's corruption ends where willingness to be ordinary begins.

chapters.title: August and the Choir
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. In August, the stars fully returned, the found family opens a waystation in Thornfell for refugees. A traveler asks the quiet man's name. 'Tamsin,' he says, remembering. 'My name is Tamsin.' Emotional beat: grace note ending; the price was paid, but not in vain, and not alone.
